About: Projectile Motion with Air Drag — Why 45° Is Wrong

Source

Simulation
Projectile Motion with Air Drag — Why 45° Is Wrong (three models on screen at once: vacuum / linear drag / quadratic drag; 🚀 Launch fires a single shot; range-vs-angle curve with marked optimum).
Concept
"45° gives maximum range" is a vacuum-only theorem: with air drag the optimum drops below 45° and the trajectory becomes asymmetric (steeper descent than ascent).
Serves
Projectile kinematics; effect of resistive forces; idealization vs realistic model; reading an optimum off a function plot.
Inquiry
Predict the best angle with drag on, then find it by experiment (θ-slider sweep with a Best-so-far tracker) and compare with the ★ optimum marked on the range-vs-angle curve.
Misconception
"45° is always the best angle" — carried by prediction choice 🅐; its rebuttal appears only when that choice is selected.
Verified anchors
g = 9.81 m/s². Vacuum, v₀ = 20 m/s, θ = 45°: R = 40.77 m, T = 2.88 s. Linear drag b = 0.3 kg/s, m = 1 kg, same launch: R = 25.26 m, optimum θ* = 39°, terminal velocity mg/b = 32.7 m/s. Quadratic drag c = 0.015 kg/m, m = 1 kg, same launch: R = 28.27 m, T = 2.59 s, optimum θ* = 42°, terminal velocity √(mg/c) = 25.6 m/s.

🎯 Projectile Motion with Air Drag

Guided Inquiry

1 · Watch the race

Press 🚀 Launch (or watch the opening shot): all three models fly together — vacuum, linear drag, and quad drag. The solid path is the Model selection; the other two ride along dotted. With drag the descent is steeper than the ascent — an asymmetry the vacuum parabola never shows — and range is shorter too.

2 · Predict the best angle

With air drag on (b > 0), which launch angle θ gives the longest shot on flat ground?

3 · Hunt the peak

Sweep the θ slider and watch Range; Best so far keeps your record. Near the top the peak is flat, so bracket it: does 35° beat 45°? Does 40°?

4 · Read it on the curve

The Range vs angle plot is open: ● is your θ, ★ is the computed optimum. At these defaults the ★ sits at 36° — your ● starts at 39°, also below the 45° reference line.

5 · What moves the ★

At stronger drag the ★ sits even lower. Raise b (or raise m and match b) and watch it slide — the flight depends on b and m only through b/m, so b = 0.30, m = 2.0 kg flies identically to b = 0.15, m = 1.0 kg. Then set b = 0 — the ★ snaps back to 45°. The "45° rule" is a vacuum-only theorem (here drag is linear, F = −b·v; real quadratic drag gives the same conclusions).

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A cannon on level ground fires a ball with launch speed v0 at angle θ. Gravity pulls it down as usual, and air drag, a force that opposes its velocity, now acts as well. The sim flies the same shot three ways at once: in a vacuum, with linear drag and with quadratic drag.

What you'll learn

  • How linear drag, F = −bv, and quadratic drag, F = −c|v|v, act on a moving ball.
  • How to read Range, Flight time, terminal speed vT and decay time τ.
  • How to test the 45° rule for longest range once drag is switched on.
The apparatus: a cannon with launch speed v0 and angle θ, and a moving ball that drag pushes against.

What's on screen

  • Vacuum path, with no air at all.
  • Linear drag path, with F = −bv.
  • Quadratic drag path, with F = −c|v|v. The model you choose is drawn solid and the other two dotted, each ending at a flag on the ground.
  • Readouts panel: Range, Best so far, Flight time, vT and τ for the chosen model.

03

Drag costs speed for as long as the ball is aloft

Drag always points against the velocity, so the ball slows as well as falling. The sim offers two laws:

linear: F = −b v    quadratic: F = −c |v| v
Both act against the velocity v. Gravity still pulls straight down with mg.

At the opening values (v0 = 29 m/s, θ = 45°, b = 0.30 kg/s, c = 0.007 kg/m, m = 1.0 kg) a vacuum shot lands 85.73 m away after 4.181 s. Linear drag lands it 44.85 m away after 3.559 s, at 16.04 m/s instead of 29.00 m/s. Quadratic drag gives 59.76 m.

Climb and fall are no longer mirror images. In vacuum the ball rises for 2.090 s, falls for 2.090 s and lands 45° below the horizontal. With linear drag it rises for 1.623 s, falls for 1.936 s and lands 63.9° below the horizontal.

See itFire at the opening values with linear drag. Watch for: three arcs, the vacuum one longest, and the drag arcs steeper on the way down.
04

Linear drag has an exact solution that depends on b/m only

With F = −bv, the velocity decays on the time scale τ = m/b, and a falling ball approaches the terminal speed vT = mg/b. The path has a closed form:

x(t) = v0xτ(1 − e−t/τ)    y(t) = (v0y + vT)τ(1 − e−t/τ) − vTt
x(t) can never pass v0xτ, so drag caps the horizontal reach.

At the opening values τ = 3.333 s, vT = 32.70 m/s and v0xτ = 68.35 m. The shot lands at 44.85 m, inside that cap.

Mass and b enter only as b/m. So b = 0.30 kg/s with m = 2.0 kg gives R = 59.61 m and T = 3.818 s, identical to b = 0.15 kg/s with m = 1.0 kg. Quadratic drag has no closed form: the sim steps it numerically, and vT = √(mg/c) = 37.44 m/s here.

See itSet b = 0.30 kg/s, m = 2.0 kg and fire. Watch for: the amber arc landing farther than at the opening values, and the Readouts showing Range 59.61 m, Flight time 3.818 s and τ 6.667 s.
05

With drag the longest shot is launched below 45°

In vacuum R = v0² sin 2θ / g, which peaks at 45° for every v0. With drag there is no such formula, so the sim computes R for each whole degree from 5° to 85° and marks the largest with ★. At the opening values ★ sits at 36° with R = 46.64 m, against 44.85 m at 45°.

Steeper arcs hang longer, and drag charges for every second aloft. Linear drag keeps 0.613 of the vacuum range at 30°, 0.523 at 45° and 0.469 at 60°. Dropping from 45° to 36° gives up 4.20 m of vacuum range but saves 5.98 m of drag loss. The peak is flat: every angle from 33° to 40° is within 1% of the best. Quadratic drag puts ★ at 42°.

θ v0

See itOpen Range vs angle and set θ = 36°. Watch for: ● sitting on ★ at 36°, left of the dashed 45° line, with Range 46.64 m.
06

Stronger drag moves the best angle lower

At v0 = 29 m/s and m = 1.0 kg, the linear-drag ★ sits at:

b (kg/s)00.100.200.300.35
★ at45°41°39°36°35°

At b = 0 there is no drag and ★ returns to 45°, so the 45° rule is a vacuum result.

Only b/m matters, so a heavier ball acts like weaker drag. Raising m to 2.0 kg at b = 0.30 kg/s moves ★ from 36° to 40°, the same as b = 0.15 kg/s at m = 1.0 kg. A slower shot also gives drag less to do: at b = 0.30 kg/s, v0 = 18 m/s puts ★ at 39°. Quadratic drag moves ★ the same way, from 45° at c = 0 to 42° at 0.007 kg/m and 40° at 0.018 kg/m.

See itOpen Range vs angle, set b = 0.35 kg/s and θ = 35°. Watch for: ★ and ● together at 35° on the plot, and Range 43.33 m in the Readouts.
07

Under drag, angles that add to 90° no longer land together

In vacuum sin 2θ = sin(180° − 2θ), so θ and 90° − θ share one range. At 29 m/s, both 30° and 60° land 74.24 m away.

Drag breaks that pairing. Linear drag gives 45.54 m at 30° but only 34.80 m at 60°. The steep shot hangs 4.243 s against 2.617 s, so drag acts on it for longer. The same happens at 36° and 54°: 46.64 m against 39.71 m.

On the Range vs angle plot, the vacuum curve is symmetric about the dashed 45° line. The drag curves peak to its left and fall faster on the steep side.

See itSet θ = 60° with linear drag and open Range vs angle. Watch for: ● on the amber curve at 60°, well below the ★ at 36°, and Range 34.80 m in the Readouts.
08

Summary

In one line. A ball flying through air keeps losing speed to drag, so its range depends on the whole flight and not on the vacuum formula alone.

Key points

  • Linear drag F = −bv has τ = m/b and vT = mg/b, with x(t) capped at v0xτ. Only b/m matters.
  • Quadratic drag F = −c|v|v has vT = √(mg/c) and is solved numerically.
  • Vacuum R = v0² sin 2θ / g peaks at 45°. With drag the best angle ★ falls below 45° and keeps falling as drag grows.

Common mix-ups

  • "45° is always the best angle." With b = 0.30 kg/s, 45° gives 44.85 m and 36° gives 46.64 m.
  • "Drag shortens every angle equally." Linear drag keeps 0.613 of the vacuum range at 30° but 0.469 at 60°.
  • "A heavier ball is slowed more." At b = 0.30 kg/s, doubling m lifts the range from 44.85 m to 59.61 m.

Things to try on your own

  • Set b = 0, sweep θ and watch ★ return to 45°.
  • Compare 30° and 60° with Vacuum, then with drag.
  • Switch to Quadratic drag and find where ★ sits.
